blocks.en: "...on this rock I will build My church, and the gates of Hades shall not prevail against it." — Matthew 16:18 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "...sobre esta roca edificaré mi iglesia; y las puertas del Hades no prevalecerán contra ella." — Mateo 16:18 (RVG)

blocks.en: Day 1 — Why Preach the Church?
blocks.es_reference: Día 1 — ¿Por qué predicar la Iglesia?

blocks.en: Of all the doctrines, this is the one your hearers think they already understand — and most of them have it wrong. Ask the average person what the church is and you will hear “the building on the corner,” or “the service I attend,” or “the club I belong to.” The preacher’s task is to replace those small pictures with the New Testament’s great one: the church is the people of God, the body of Christ, the temple of the Spirit.
blocks.es_reference: De todas las doctrinas, esta es la que sus oyentes creen ya entender — y la mayoría la tiene equivocada. Pregunte a la persona común qué es la iglesia y oirá “el edificio de la esquina,” o “el servicio al que asisto,” o “el club al que pertenezco.” La tarea del predicador es reemplazar esas imágenes pequeñas por la gran imagen del Nuevo Testamento: la iglesia es el pueblo de Dios, el cuerpo de Cristo, el templo del Espíritu.

blocks.en: So the pastoral aim is to move hearers from attending to belonging, and from belonging to mission. A sermon on the church should leave a person no longer asking “what do I get from this service?” but “who am I as part of this people, and what am I for?”
blocks.es_reference: Así que el objetivo pastoral es mover a los oyentes de asistir a pertenecer, y de pertenecer a la misión. Un sermón sobre la iglesia debe dejar a la persona ya no preguntando “¿qué recibo de este servicio?” sino “¿quién soy como parte de este pueblo, y para qué existo?”

blocks.en: "...on this rock I will build My church, and the gates of Hades shall not prevail against it." — Matthew 16:18 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "...sobre esta roca edificaré mi iglesia; y las puertas del Hades no prevalecerán contra ella." — Mateo 16:18 (RVG)

blocks.en: Day 2 — The Doctrinal Backbone (lean; see Systematic Theology Unit 8)
blocks.es_reference: Día 2 — El fundamento doctrinal (breve; vea Teología Sistemática, Unidad 8)

blocks.en: Hold the doctrine before shaping it. Keep it compressed and point students to ST Unit 8 for the full treatment. The nature of the church. The church is not a building but the people God has called out: the people of God, the body of Christ with Christ as Head, and the temple indwelt by the Spirit. It is both universal (all believers of all ages) and local (the gathered congregation). The mission of the church. Three tasks run through the New Testament: worship toward God, edification of one another, and evangelism toward the world — the Great Commission of Matthew 28:19–20. The ordinances. Two were given by Christ: baptism, which pictures union with Him in death and resurrection (Romans 6:3–4), and the Lord’s Supper, which proclaims His death until He comes (1 Corinthians 11:26). The course keeps its ecclesiology deliberately non-denominational, naming what all believers share rather than what divides them.
blocks.es_reference: Sostenga la doctrina antes de darle forma. Manténgala comprimida y remita a los alumnos a la Unidad 8 de TS para el tratamiento completo. La naturaleza de la iglesia. La iglesia no es un edificio sino el pueblo que Dios ha llamado: el pueblo de Dios, el cuerpo de Cristo con Cristo como Cabeza, y el templo en que mora el Espíritu. Es a la vez universal (todos los creyentes de todas las edades) y local (la congregación reunida). La misión de la iglesia. Tres tareas recorren el Nuevo Testamento: la adoración hacia Dios, la edificación mutua, y la evangelización hacia el mundo — la Gran Comisión de Mateo 28:19–20. Las ordenanzas. Cristo dio dos: el bautismo, que representa la unión con Él en muerte y resurrección (Romanos 6:3–4), y la Cena del Señor, que proclama su muerte hasta que Él venga (1 Corintios 11:26). El curso mantiene su eclesiología deliberadamente no denominacional, nombrando lo que todos los creyentes comparten en lugar de lo que los divide.

blocks.en: Day 3 — The Homiletical Move (a textual sermon opening into topical)
blocks.es_reference: Día 3 — El movimiento homilético (un sermón textual que se abre a lo tópico)

blocks.en: Units 3 through 8 mostly began with a subject and gathered texts to it (topical). Here is the other road from Unit 2: start inside one text and let its own clauses become the points. This is the textual method opening naturally into a topical naming of ideas. The worked example is adapted from Dr. Cook’s sermon “The Identity of the Gathered.”
blocks.es_reference: Las Unidades 3 a 8 mayormente comenzaron con un tema y reunieron textos hacia él (tópico). Aquí está el otro camino de la Unidad 2: comenzar dentro de un texto y dejar que sus propias cláusulas se vuelvan los puntos. Este es el método textual abriéndose naturalmente a un nombramiento tópico de ideas. El ejemplo desarrollado está adaptado del sermón del Dr. Cook “La Identidad de los Reunidos.”

blocks.en: "But you are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, His own special people, that you may proclaim the praises of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvelous light." — 1 Peter 2:9 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Mas vosotros sois linaje escogido, real sacerdocio, nación santa, pueblo adquirido, para que anunciéis las virtudes de aquel que os llamó de las tinieblas a su luz admirable." — 1 Pedro 2:9 (RVG)

blocks.en: Subject: who the church is. Interrogative: “What does God call His gathered people?” Keyword: identities. The four points are the four clauses of the one verse, each a name God gives His people:
blocks.es_reference: Tema: quién es la iglesia. Interrogativo: “¿Cómo llama Dios a su pueblo reunido?” Palabra clave: identidades. Los cuatro puntos son las cuatro cláusulas del solo versículo, cada una un nombre que Dios da a su pueblo:

blocks.en: Point (keyword: identities)Clause of 1 Peter 2:9
blocks.es_reference: Punto (palabra clave: identidades)Cláusula de 1 Pedro 2:9

blocks.en: 1. A chosen generation — a people God chose for Himself"a chosen generation"
blocks.es_reference: 1. Linaje escogido — un pueblo que Dios escogió para Sí"linaje escogido"

blocks.en: 2. A royal priesthood — every believer has access and a ministry"a royal priesthood"
blocks.es_reference: 2. Real sacerdocio — cada creyente tiene acceso y ministerio"real sacerdocio"

blocks.en: 3. A holy nation — a people set apart for God"a holy nation"
blocks.es_reference: 3. Nación santa — un pueblo apartado para Dios"nación santa"

blocks.en: 4. His own special people — God’s treasured possession"His own special people"
blocks.es_reference: 4. Pueblo adquirido — la posesión atesorada de Dios"pueblo adquirido"

blocks.en: Take each name in turn, for each tells the gathered people something true about who they are.
blocks.es_reference: Considere cada nombre por turno, pues cada uno dice al pueblo reunido algo verdadero sobre quién es.

blocks.en: 1. A chosen generation. Chosen, elected, predestined — these are good biblical words, and we will not flinch from them. But we must preach them the way Scripture does. Scripture never once says God chose anyone for hell; it says the very opposite — God is “not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance” (2 Peter 3:9). He does not look down upon a child in the womb and decree its damnation. He foreknows all things, yes — but foreknowledge is not the same as predestining a soul to be lost. And the best-known verse in all the Bible holds the truth out to everyone: “God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son, that whoever believes in Him should not perish but have everlasting life” (John 3:16). The door stands open to whoever will come, and when one comes, the angels of heaven rejoice (Luke 15:10). And here is why this matters for the gathered church: take election so far that every soul is settled beyond recall, and you cut the nerve of missions — for why carry the gospel across the world if no one’s eternity can turn on the hearing of it? That is the very logic that once told a young William Carey to sit down, that God would save the heathen without his help. Carey would not sit down, and neither must we. We preach a real choosing by a sovereign God and a real “whosoever,” because the gospel is for the world. So preach election as the warm truth it is — that God has chosen a people for Himself — and never as a cold decree that bolts the door God has thrown open.
blocks.es_reference: 1. Linaje escogido. Escogido, elegido, predestinado — son buenas palabras bíblicas, y no las rehuiremos. Pero hemos de predicarlas como las predica la Escritura. La Escritura nunca dice que Dios escogiera a nadie para el infierno; dice lo contrario — Dios “no queriendo que ninguno perezca, sino que todos vengan al arrepentimiento” (2 Pedro 3:9). Él no mira a un niño en el vientre y decreta su condenación. Conoce de antemano todas las cosas, sí — pero el conocimiento anticipado no es lo mismo que predestinar un alma a perderse. Y el versículo más conocido de toda la Biblia ofrece la verdad a todos: “de tal manera amó Dios al mundo, que ha dado a su Hijo unigénito, para que todo aquel que en Él cree no se pierda, mas tenga vida eterna” (Juan 3:16). La puerta está abierta a todo el que quiera venir, y cuando uno viene, los ángeles del cielo se gozan (Lucas 15:10). Y he aquí por qué esto importa para la iglesia reunida: lleve la elección tan lejos que toda alma quede fijada sin remedio, y cortará el nervio de las misiones — pues ¿para qué llevar el evangelio por el mundo si la eternidad de nadie puede depender de oírlo? Esa es la lógica que una vez dijo a un joven William Carey que se sentara, que Dios salvaría a los paganos sin su ayuda. Carey no se sentó, y tampoco nosotros debemos hacerlo. Predicamos una elección real por un Dios soberano y un “todo aquel” real, porque el evangelio es para el mundo. Así que predique la elección como la cálida verdad que es — que Dios ha escogido un pueblo para Sí — y nunca como un frío decreto que cierra la puerta que Dios ha abierto de par en par.

blocks.en: 2. A royal priesthood. This identity is developed in full below as the worked example — every believer brought near, with direct access to God and a real ministry to others, and no spiritual middle-man standing between the soul and the Father.
blocks.es_reference: 2. Real sacerdocio. Esta identidad se desarrolla por completo abajo como el ejemplo — cada creyente acercado, con acceso directo a Dios y un ministerio real hacia otros, y ningún intermediario espiritual entre el alma y el Padre.

blocks.en: 3. A holy nation. The word holy means set apart. These people are a nation within the nations, citizens of a kingdom not of this world, living under a different law and a different King. They are in the world but not of it — not better than their neighbors by nature, but claimed and set apart by God for His own purposes. A church that looks exactly like the world around it has forgotten this name; the gathered people are meant to be visibly different, not in pride but in holiness.
blocks.es_reference: 3. Nación santa. La palabra santa significa apartada. Este pueblo es una nación dentro de las naciones, ciudadanos de un reino que no es de este mundo, viviendo bajo una ley distinta y un Rey distinto. Están en el mundo pero no son del mundo — no mejores que sus vecinos por naturaleza, sino reclamados y apartados por Dios para sus propios propósitos. Una iglesia que se ve exactamente igual que el mundo a su alrededor ha olvidado este nombre; el pueblo reunido ha de ser visiblemente diferente, no por orgullo sino en santidad.

blocks.en: 4. His own special people. The older word is peculiar — not strange, but treasured, a personal possession a king keeps for himself. Of all that God owns — and He owns everything — He calls His people His treasure. The hearer who has felt unwanted his whole life is told the astonishing thing: the God of heaven counts him among His prized possessions, purchased at the price of His Son’s own blood and kept as His own forever.
blocks.es_reference: 4. Pueblo adquirido. La palabra antigua es peculiar — no extraño, sino atesorado, una posesión personal que un rey guarda para sí. De todo lo que Dios posee — y lo posee todo — llama a su pueblo su tesoro. Al oyente que se ha sentido no deseado toda su vida se le dice lo asombroso: el Dios del cielo lo cuenta entre sus posesiones más preciadas, comprado al precio de la propia sangre de su Hijo y guardado como suyo para siempre.

blocks.en: And the verse supplies its own conclusion. The closing clause — “that you may proclaim the praises of Him who called you” — turns identity into mission. Who the church is drives what the church is for.
blocks.es_reference: Y el versículo aporta su propia conclusión. La cláusula final — “para que anunciéis las virtudes de aquel que os llamó” — convierte la identidad en misión. Quién es la iglesia impulsa para qué existe la iglesia.

blocks.en: Day 4 — Developing a Point (E-A-I) and an Illustration Bank
blocks.es_reference: Día 4 — Desarrollando un punto (E-A-I) y un banco de ilustraciones

blocks.en: Here is Point 2, the royal priesthood, developed in full:
blocks.es_reference: He aquí el Punto 2, el real sacerdocio, desarrollado por completo:

blocks.en: Explanation of the text. Under the old covenant only priests came near to God, and only one priest entered the holiest place once a year. Peter says the whole people is now a royal priesthood: through Christ every believer has direct access to God and a real ministry to others. No spiritual middle-man stands between you and the Father.
blocks.es_reference: Explicación del texto. Bajo el antiguo pacto solo los sacerdotes se acercaban a Dios, y solo un sacerdote entraba al lugar santísimo una vez al año. Pedro dice que ahora todo el pueblo es un real sacerdocio: por medio de Cristo cada creyente tiene acceso directo a Dios y un ministerio real hacia los demás. Ningún intermediario espiritual se interpone entre usted y el Padre.

blocks.en: Application of the text. This means there are no spectators in the church. The believer in the pew is not a customer of religion but a priest with work to do — to pray, to bring others to God, to offer his life as worship. If you have been waiting for “the ministry” to do the work, this verse hands the work to you.
blocks.es_reference: Aplicación del texto. Esto significa que no hay espectadores en la iglesia. El creyente en la banca no es un cliente de la religión sino un sacerdote con obra que hacer — orar, traer a otros a Dios, ofrecer su vida como adoración. Si ha estado esperando que “el ministerio” haga la obra, este versículo le entrega la obra a usted.

blocks.en: Illustration. In a great house there are guests who are served and there is family who serve. The royal priesthood means you have been moved from guest to family — you have a key to the door and a place at the work, not just a seat at the table.
blocks.es_reference: Ilustración. En una gran casa hay invitados a quienes se sirve y hay familia que sirve. El real sacerdocio significa que usted ha sido movido de invitado a familia — tiene una llave de la puerta y un lugar en la obra, no solo un asiento en la mesa.

blocks.en: The other three identities are developed the same way. Illustrations for the church are plentiful — use the bank:
blocks.es_reference: Las otras tres identidades se desarrollan igual. Las ilustraciones para la iglesia abundan — use el banco:

blocks.en: 💡 Living Stones: Peter says believers are “living stones, being built up a spiritual house” (1 Peter 2:5). A stone alone in a field is just a stone; set into the wall it becomes part of something that shelters and stands. You were not saved to lie alone in a field.
blocks.es_reference: 💡 Piedras Vivas: Pedro dice que los creyentes son “piedras vivas, edificados como casa espiritual” (1 Pedro 2:5). Una piedra sola en un campo es solo una piedra; puesta en el muro se vuelve parte de algo que abriga y permanece. Usted no fue salvo para yacer solo en un campo.

blocks.en: 💡 One Body, Many Members: Paul’s picture in 1 Corinthians 12 — the hand cannot say to the eye, “I have no need of you.” The church is one body whose members need each other; a severed hand is not independent, it is dead.
blocks.es_reference: 💡 Un Cuerpo, Muchos Miembros: la imagen de Pablo en 1 Corintios 12 — la mano no puede decir al ojo, “no te necesito.” La iglesia es un cuerpo cuyos miembros se necesitan unos a otros; una mano cortada no es independiente, está muerta.

blocks.en: Day 5 — Craft Notes and Summary
blocks.es_reference: Día 5 — Notas de oficio y resumen

blocks.en: Two cautions. Do not preach an organizational chart. The temptation is to spend the sermon on church government, committees, and structures; those have their place, but a sermon on the church should send people away knowing who they are, not how the bylaws read. Preach toward belonging and serving. Because identity drives mission, the natural arc of a church sermon is an invitation to stop spectating: to belong to the people, take up the priesthood, and join the work. That is the response the text itself reaches for.
blocks.es_reference: Dos advertencias. No prediques un organigrama. La tentación es gastar el sermón en el gobierno de la iglesia, los comités y las estructuras; eso tiene su lugar, pero un sermón sobre la iglesia debe enviar a la gente sabiendo quiénes son, no cómo dicen los estatutos. Predica hacia el pertenecer y el servir. Porque la identidad impulsa la misión, el arco natural de un sermón sobre la iglesia es una invitación a dejar de ser espectador: pertenecer al pueblo, tomar el sacerdocio y unirse a la obra. Esa es la respuesta que el texto mismo busca.

blocks.en: So Unit 9 showed the second road of the method: a textual sermon that begins inside one verse and lets its clauses become the points, naming the church’s identities and ending where the verse ends — in mission. Unit 10 brings the course home with the doctrine of Last Things.
blocks.es_reference: Así que la Unidad 9 mostró el segundo camino del método: un sermón textual que comienza dentro de un versículo y deja que sus cláusulas se vuelvan los puntos, nombrando las identidades de la iglesia y terminando donde termina el versículo — en la misión. La Unidad 10 lleva el curso a casa con la doctrina de las Últimas Cosas.

sa.prompt: Why preach the doctrine of the church, and what is the pastoral aim of such a sermon?
sa.model: We preach the church because it is the doctrine hearers think they already understand, yet most reduce it to a building, a service they attend, or a club they belong to. The pastoral aim is to replace those small pictures with the New Testament’s great one and to move people from attending to belonging, and from belonging to mission. A good sermon on the church leaves a person no longer asking what they get from the service but who they are as part of this people and what they are for. So the aim is identity and mission: to know oneself as part of the people of God and to take up the work of serving.

sa.prompt: What is the church according to the New Testament, and what does it mean that it is both universal and local?
sa.model: According to the New Testament the church is not a building but the people God has called out: the people of God, the body of Christ with Christ as its Head, and the temple indwelt by the Holy Spirit. It is universal in that it includes all believers of all ages everywhere, and local in that it appears as the gathered congregation in a particular place. Both are true at once: every local church is an expression of the one universal people, and the believer belongs to the whole body even as he belongs to a specific congregation. So to preach the church rightly is to lift people’s eyes from the building to the people, and from their own congregation to the worldwide family of God.

sa.prompt: Lay out the worked example on 1 Peter 2:9: text, subject, interrogative, keyword, and why it is textual opening into topical.
sa.model: The text is 1 Peter 2:9. The subject is who the church is. The interrogative asked of it is, what does God call His gathered people? The keyword that answers is identities, and the four points are the four clauses of the one verse: a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, and His own special people. It is a textual sermon because it begins inside a single verse and lets that verse’s own clauses become the points, rather than gathering many scattered texts. It opens into the topical because those clauses are then named and arranged as identities of the church. The verse even supplies the conclusion, since its closing clause turns identity into mission.

sa.prompt: Name the four identities of the church in 1 Peter 2:9 and what each one means.
sa.model: The verse gives the church four identities. A chosen generation means a people God chose for Himself, not one that chose itself. A royal priesthood means that through Christ every believer has direct access to God and a real ministry, with no spiritual middle-man between the believer and the Father. A holy nation means a people set apart for God, belonging to Him and marked by His holiness. And His own special people means God’s treasured possession, a people He purchased and prizes as His own. Four names, all from one verse, each describing who the gathered people of God truly are.

sa.prompt: Develop “a royal priesthood” as a sermon point using Explanation, Application, and Illustration.
sa.model: The Explanation is that under the old covenant only priests came near to God and only one entered the holiest place once a year, but Peter says the whole people is now a royal priesthood, so through Christ every believer has direct access to God and a real ministry, with no middle-man between the believer and the Father. The Application is that there are no spectators in the church; the believer in the pew is not a customer of religion but a priest with work to do, to pray, to bring others to God, and to offer his life as worship, so the work is handed to him rather than left to the clergy. The Illustration is that in a great house there are guests who are served and family who serve, and the royal priesthood means you have been moved from guest to family, with a key to the door and a place at the work, not just a seat at the table.

sa.prompt: Explain how the church’s identity leads to its mission, using the closing clause of 1 Peter 2:9.
sa.model: The verse does not stop at naming who the church is; it gives a purpose. After calling the people a chosen generation, royal priesthood, holy nation, and special possession, it adds the closing clause: that you may proclaim the praises of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvelous light. So identity leads directly to mission. The church is not chosen and set apart for its own comfort but in order to declare God’s praises to the world. Who the church is drives what the church is for, and the experience of being called out of darkness into light is exactly what the church now proclaims. A sermon that names the identities and stops short of this purpose has left the verse half-preached.

sa.prompt: Describe the two ordinances of the church and what each one pictures or proclaims.
sa.model: Christ gave the church two ordinances. Baptism pictures the believer’s union with Christ in His death and resurrection: going down into the water and rising again portrays dying to the old life and rising to new life, as Romans 6:3–4 teaches. The Lord’s Supper proclaims the Lord’s death until He comes, as 1 Corinthians 11:26 says: the bread and the cup set His sacrifice before the eyes of the church again and again until His return. So one ordinance marks the beginning of the Christian life and the other sustains and proclaims it, and both are acted sermons, the truth made visible in what the church does together.

sa.prompt: What is the mission of the church? Name its three tasks.
sa.model: The mission of the church runs in three directions through the New Testament. First is worship, the church’s task toward God, gathering to honor and adore Him. Second is edification, the task toward one another, building up the members of the body so they grow and serve. Third is evangelism, the task toward the world, carrying the gospel to those outside, which is the Great Commission of Matthew 28:19–20 to make disciples of all nations. Worship looks up, edification looks in, and evangelism looks out, and a healthy church gives itself to all three rather than collapsing into only one.

sa.prompt: Give two cautions for preaching the church, and explain why the sermon should arc toward belonging and serving.
sa.model: One caution is not to preach an organizational chart, spending the sermon on church government, committees, and structures; those have their place but should not crowd out the truth of who the people are. A second caution is to keep the doctrine non-denominational, naming what all believers share rather than what divides them. The sermon should arc toward belonging and serving because identity drives mission: once a hearer sees that he is part of the chosen people and a member of the royal priesthood, the natural response is to stop being a spectator, to belong to the people, and to take up the work. So the invitation is not merely to attend but to join the body and serve, which is exactly where the text itself is heading.

sa.prompt: Summarize how Unit 9 runs the method on the doctrine of the church.
sa.model: Unit 9 takes the doctrine of the church and runs the method by its second road. It begins with a lean backbone from systematic theology: the church is the people of God, the body of Christ, and the temple of the Spirit, with a mission of worship, edification, and evangelism and the two ordinances of baptism and the Lord’s Supper. Then it makes the homiletical move as a textual sermon: the subject is who the church is, the keyword is identities, and the four points are the four clauses of one verse, 1 Peter 2:9. One point, the royal priesthood, is developed by Explanation, Application, and Illustration. Finally the sermon ends where the verse ends, in mission, since identity drives the call to belong and serve. Backbone, a textual-into-topical move, a worked point, and an arc to response: the same template, run from inside a single text.
